utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber would like to invite the parties to address the matters of the notes, having now seen the original one will be returned to the Prosecution as they provided it. The parties are invited to address the Court not more than five minutes on the matter how to proceed at this very moment. If you could do it in less than five minutes, that would be appreciated. May I take it that the matter is equal for all Defence counsel; that doesn't make any difference whether it's Mr. Haradinaj or Mr. Brahimaj or Mr. Balaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can deal with it I hope in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is Your Honours will have seen the copies and translations I hope of the contents of the notebook. Comparisons have been made between those notes and the notes that were supplied in December. There is no verbatim information from the December notes that appears in the notebook. There are two pages where there is some similar information, but it's limited to one line on one page and two pieces of information on another page, which essentially are the dates on which this witness made his OTP witness statement. So other than those two isolated examples, all of the information in the notebook comes from some source other than the notes that were supplied in December. In terms of practical proposals - and we're all anxious to reduce delay, for obvious reasons, as much as possible - we've discussed the matter between ourselves. The suggestion we put forward for the Chamber's consideration is that we proceed now with examination-in-chief and with Mr. Kearney keeping as far as he can to the time estimate with cross-examination. We then break and depending upon whether Your Honours wish to conclude cross-examination tomorrow or -- or at some later stage. The witness, as I understand it, has not been able to obtain the notes overnight. It may be that the most convenient thing would be to break at the end of the session today, for the witness to obtain his notes, and then to return for further cross-examination if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say let's proceed with examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and, if need be, re-call for cross-examination once we have received everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think one would expect him to return after the break with his notes, then to be examined; and then, in fact, if there is rise for cross-examination, for the cross-examination to be concluded at that stage, if Your Honours are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you're talking about the break, you mean the break of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's our understanding also. Mr. Emmerson and I has a long talk this morning about the matter, and we feel that we should just go as far as we can today. Hopefully, we can finish the direct examination and perhaps a good portion of cross. Let the witness go home, gather every note he can possibly find, come back with them, and then we can finish the matter at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will decide at a later stage whether we now already decide that he should return to the Hague with the notes, or whether he's expected to send the notes to The Hague, and then we'll then consider whether or not he's needed here in The Hague for further cross-examination. It is as if the parties could have read the mind of the Chamber. The Chamber, of course, has considered the matter well in advance and was inclined to find a similar solution but first wanted to hear the parties about it. We'll proceed as suggested by the parties, and the witness will be instructed to deliver in one way or another, through the Victims and Witnesses Section most likely, his notes to The Hague after he has returned home. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Kearney, in the present circumstances, of course, the Chamber would very much appreciate if you would strictly adhere to time assessments, if you would even be able to gain a bit of time that would enhance the possibility that we would finish with the -- I would say the normal line of examination-in-chief and cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll do the best we can. Obviously, there is substantial material to elicit from this witness, however. So we'll go as fast as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated, Witness 29. I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday still binds you; that means that you still have to answer all questions in accordance with the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. You'll now be examined by Mr. Kearney, and we now move on, not just about notes but about what happened at the time. Mr. Kearney, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And with the Court's permission, I'd like to call up, if I may, 65 ter number 1312. This is the 92 ter statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the nine-paragraph 92 ter statement. Perhaps I could already ask the Defence whether there's any objection against admission of.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's none, so let's first hear the witness answer the questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, do you see a document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, Witness 29?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise both your name and your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The name, as shown now, and signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see my name, my signature, and some of my notes, and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I wonder if we could show the witness the actual text of that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be on the next page -- no. It says this is 1 page out of 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, please take a look at the nine paragraphs there reflected in that statement, and I would like to ask you, first of all, if you recognise what is being discussed in those paragraphs and if those are your true words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I see here is part of the statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And the information contained in that document, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information I gave is accurate from all the things that I remembered. I don't know if I forgot anything. It's been a long time, and maybe I forgot some minor detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: If you were asked those same questions today in court, would you give those same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me the same questions today, maybe I might have forgotten some of the things, minor things, that have happened, but I think 95 per cent of what I said I will say again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. This statement you are now looking at is the statement which you gave in this month when you arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a statement I gave some time ago, not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. Mr. Kearney, could you, please, because I see on the -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I can clear it up, Your Honour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I see now where the problem lies. If you look at the Albanian version, Mr. Kearney, and that's the one shown to the witness -- could we go back to the first page of this document. You see the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which is now a translation from English into Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's 23rd of April, 2007; whereas, the English original says 23rd of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's a -- in this case, Your Honours, the Albanian version is correct. What happened is -- perhaps I can ask the witness to take his headphones off if the Court would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought this was the consolidated new statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. What happened is this witness made an earlier statement in 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: These nine paragraphs were taken from them almost verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.. They are excerpts rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes. And then this week, he was shown those nine paragraphs and asked to sign, again. In the English translation of the document that was made just this week, the date on the front of the translation of the document says "2006," when it should have said "2007." The Albanian is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I can ask him some more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you can please clarify that with him. Of course, I now better understand why he says it was quite some time ago, because the text he gave was quite some time ago, although it was confirmed or renewed this week. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, the text of the document you have in front of you, those paragraphs was information given to you -- or given by you to the Office of the Prosecutor back some time ago, in 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: But just this week, two days ago, we took part of that initial statement you gave and put it into this smaller document and had you sign it two days ago. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Or three days ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was two or three days ago, but I know that we made a small intervention. I was given the opportunity to read the statement again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: In any event, two or three days ago when you signed this new statement, you read it again and did you, before you signed it, confirm that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it; and after I read it, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would, at this point, tender this document, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have heard already from the Defence that there's no objection; therefore, the document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have it -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P263, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, obviously, that matter is under seal. Is that right? That document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar said that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, I have a short summary of those paragraphs that I would be prepared to read into the record at this time. I've given counsel a copy of that this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is important that it will be read, but let's not spend time on it at this very moment. It's to inform the public, but that could be done on a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, I would now like to get into your testimony if we may, and, specifically, I want to talk to you about your knowledge of the FARK's activities in 1998. And I'd like to ask you, first, as a starting point: Were you a member of the FARK in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you've told us in your statement that you were a common soldier, but did you have any special duties within the FARK army in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998, I was a simple soldier, but at the same time I also had duties that were not the duties of a simple soldier. The people I worked with during 1998 were all superior officers who had military academy formation, and they tasked me with some duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the Defence if it is not about actually what the witness saw, et cetera, but about his position, whether there's any objection against leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, in a certain area, leading will not find any objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And those commanders that you had contact with were Sali Ceku and Tahir Zemaj. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What special duties did Mr. Ceku and Mr. Zemaj give to you during 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1998, I can't remember the exact date now, I was given the duty to go from Albania to Kosovo several times to see what the situation was like; then later I was given other duties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, these entries that you made into Kosovo to see what the situation was like, that was before the formal entry of the FARK into Kosovo. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Just so we know a time-frame, what was the entry date of the FARK -- the formal entry date of the FARK into Kosovo in 1998, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the 25th and the 26th; of course, as I say, as far as I remember, because I can't be a hundred per cent sure about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon. The 25th and 26th of which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25th and 26th of June. It was June, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that before that June entry date of the FARK into Kosovo, you were tasked to see what the situation in Kosovo was like. Could you please expand on that. What specifically were you -- you looking to see at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I went there to see what the situation was like. Later on, when some movements of the KLA started, we were interested to know how the things were developing, how ready the population was to defend themselves, and if it was a situation where we could fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many of these entries into Kosovo did you make before the main body of the FARK entered Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered approximately ten times, maybe more, but I'm sure about ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How long would these trips last typically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended how long the trip would take. Sometimes the journey took three to ten days. It depended on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Would you go by yourself or with other FARK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some occasions, I took two or three of my comrades with me. Sometimes I also went alone. It depended on the task I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And these ten visits we're talking about in 1998, over what span of time were they, sir? When did you begin making these entries into Kosovo and -- let me ask that date. When did you begin making these entries into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was in January 1998. The last time was, if I'm not mistaken, a few days before we entered with the FARK forces in Kosovo, but I'm not sure how many days earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What zone of Kosovo were you entering during that period of time? Where were you focusing your efforts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually in some villages of the municipality of Gjakove and in the municipality of Decane. It was impossible to visit all the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that you were assessing in part the KLA. Were you also assessing Serb activity in the area during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I was able to assess their movements, of course, it would be a very good thing; but it was very difficult for me to assess them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult because at the time the KLA had started its own movements, and also the Army of Yugoslavia had started its own movements. So it was very difficult for me to enter in areas where the JNA dominated. That's why I mainly moved in the areas where the KLA was in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What area were those that the KLA was in control, and please tell us -- give us a time reference if you can of the statements you're making now. You said you began going into Kosovo in January, and you continued making trips all the way up through June. This last question I asked you about areas of KLA dominance. Please tell us, when you tell us where, tell us also when, what time-period you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning - I'm speaking about January 1998 - the KLA had not emerged yet, and the Army of Yugoslavia was not openly operating. It was only the police that was operating. So it was easier for me to go from village to village, and even the other citizens could move more freely; then later on, the KLA emerged, the situation exacerbated between the KLA and the Serb forces. And that's why my movements became even more difficult. Also the movements of the population became more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, again, Witness 29, please tell us what time-frame you're talking about. When you say the KLA emerged and the situation between they and the Serb forces exacerbated, what time-frame are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring, if I'm not wrong, to the period from 24th of March onwards; and then the KLA appeared, as I said, and the circumstances changed. I always want to emphasise the fact that I might make some mistakes on the-- about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that you noticed in your travels through Kosovo in early 1998 that there were -- or in 1998 that there were areas of KLA domination. I want to ask you: After March 24th, after their emergence in your mind, what were the areas of KLA domination that you encountered yourself during your travels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before March, as I said, the KLA was not present. After March, there were some villages where it dominated, some others which were free in the sense of there were no enemy forces or large KLA forces. Only some preparations for self-defense by the peasants were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What were the villages where you noticed KLA dominance after March 24th of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After March 1998, initially, it appeared in Gllogjan, if I'm not mistaken; and then, gradually, it started to spread out mostly in the Decane villages. But I cannot be very certain as to its appearance and to what village it did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During your trips - I want to confine my time-frame now between March 24th, 1998, and the end of June 1998, when the FARK forces entered Kosovo - during that period of time, what villages do you remember going to where there was a KLA presence or a KLA domination, as you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 24th of March that we are talking about, initially, as I said, it emerged in Gllogjan village and then in all the villages -- almost all the villages of Decane commune. In some villages more; in some villages less. I can't specify where it was more present. But beginning from the 24th of March, as I said, it emerged in Gllogjan and all its villages, and after that in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, in your 2002 statement, Witness 29, you list specific villages that you visited during this time-period. I'm just going to read those to you. I'm going to ask you, first of all, these were villages you actually did visit during that time-frame between March and June of 1998. The first one was Smolice. Did you visit that village during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once I crossed the border, that's the first village that you run into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Then you listed Ponashec, P-o-n-a-s-h-e-c?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ponashec, too, lies next to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Then you visited Racaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Junik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Herec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Gramaqel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Rznic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you notice a KLA dominance in any or all of those villages during the time-period between March and June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In these villages and in many other villages that I visited, there was a KLA dominance, while the enemy forces moved along the main roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During your movement among these villages during this time-period, did you notice KLA activity in these villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was the beginning. I mostly saw armed people; some of them being without uniforms, some being in uniform. As I said, they were kind of preparations to form the army; then I contacted some representatives of the villages. Those people told me they were the senior people in the village. I wished to meet them and talk to them, but I also talked with ordinary soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because, in my opinion, all were equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say senior people -- you talked to senior people in the villages, are you referring to senior people within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What were the -- these senior people in the villages, what were they called or what did you refer to them to? Were they village commanders? Were they officers? Were they soldiers? How did you refer to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some villages, it was a representative of the village or, if I might say, the commander of the village. In some villages, there was a commander for all of them. So there were different, let's say, organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: These village commanders or these KLA village commanders, when did they start -- in your own experience, when did they start appearing in these villages? When did you start noticing that activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always, if I am right, after the 24th of March, and kept growing and spreading out every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: As you travelled at the village level through villages in the Dukadjin area between March and June of 1998, was it your habit routinely to make contact with the KLA village commanders in these villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- I'm going to object to the issue of whether it was habit. He can tell us what he did and how he - excuse me, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and how he proceeded. But what his habit was at this juncture I think is a bit much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, you could ask for a habit by just rephrasing that question: Did you usually go there or did you at all times. So therefore it is a minor issue. Mr. Kearney, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My only concern is how one treats a habit evidence at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was it your usual practice -- did you usually make contact with KLA village commanders during this time-period when you entered villages in the Dukadjin Zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to make as many contacts as I possibly could with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Why was that, Witness 29?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wished to get the right idea of the situation, of the current situation then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you say a "right idea of the current situation," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this I mean that I wished to meet them, but it was also part of my duty given to me by my superior people, because we wanted to get to -- to have a very clear and correct idea of the situation of what was going on. For this, we needed to meet the -- what were called then commanders of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During these discussions with the village -- the KLA village commanders and soldiers, did you learn who the overall KLA commander was for that region at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Or maybe before that, if there was an overall commander; and then if yes, who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, let me rephrase that question. During this time-period, between March 24th and late June of 1998, in your discussions with both KLA soldiers and village commanders, did you learn if there was a KLA overall commander for the Dukadjini Zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not the entire Dukagjin Zone was in a state of war, but most of Decane commune and part of Gjakove municipality. But each and every one were saying that Ramush Haradinaj was the overall commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Was Ramush Haradinaj someone who was known to you, Witness 29, at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him -- would you please repeat the question, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Certainly. When you started hearing that the overall commander was Ramush Haradinaj during that time-period in 1998, I just want to ask you simply: Before that time, before 1998, did you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him since a long time ago. I used to know Mr. Haradinaj since we -- since when we were ten or 12 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And how was it you knew him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know Mr. Haradinaj. We -- our villages were close to each other. Besides that, we went to the same school. I wouldn't say that we were classmates, but we were going to the same school. We lived very close to each other and we used to see each other, sometimes talk with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many years -- first of all, what was the age difference or what is the age difference between you and Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I am older than him, maybe two, three years older. I wouldn't say that I'm older than three years; two or three, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you attend the same schools when you were growing up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And we had good social relationship. We weren't very close friends, maybe because I was a little bit older. We were not in the same class, but each had his own close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: How many years did you attend the same schools together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Haradinaj, we went to the same school for eight years to what we referred to as the primary school or the low-cycle school, and then two years in the high school; and then Mr. Haradinaj went to another place. I went somewhere else. I don't know anymore what happened with him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So during those ten-year period when you went to the same schools together, how often would you see him? Was it a daily basis? A weekly basis? A monthly basis? Please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, please. Sometimes we saw him several times a day, sometimes once a week, but the fact is that we were in the same school. We were neighbours and we met sometimes, as I said, a couple of times a day; sometimes once a day; sometimes -- sometimes a week. But I -- we did know each other very well. So we are, I would say, kind of friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you also know his brother Daut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did know Daut, too. I knew some of his brothers but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, I now want to move back to the entry of the FARK into Kosovo. You said that this occurred in late June of 1998. I believe you told us it was either the 24th or 26th of June. Am I stating that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: 25th or 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The 25th or 26th of June. First of all, is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon. Actually, it was the 25th and 26th that was how it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, do you have the question in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date when the FARK forces left the barracks, it was the 24th. They stayed for one day in the Tropoja Mountains during the 25th; and in the evening of the 25th, after darkness fell, they left towards Kosova. On the 26th, we entered Kosova; that is, the 26th found us in Kosova because it was past midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Describe the size of the force, please, if you will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you accurate figures because it was not part of my duty to count them; but when we entered Kosova, I think we were about -- from 120 to 150 soldiers, including 21 officers; that is, the number was from 120 to 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the armament that you brought with you when you came into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had not heavy weapons. We had, I think, what we described as Kalashnikov rifles. Our senior officers had a pistol, the soldiers had automatic guns; then we had some other weapons, but not heavy weapons because we were walking on foot, and it was impossible for us to carry heavy weapons. We were a large number of soldiers and officers, and the commanders didn't want us to carry these weapons by animals. First, the decision was for us to enter Kosova and then transport heavier weapons afterwards. And each of the soldiers and officers had his personal equipment, the munitions of the weapon itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And, Witness 29, what was your purpose in entering Kosovo? Who were you going to fight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear that we entered Kosova to stand up for our people, to defend them from the enemy, from the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, did you go to a particular village when you first entered Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, in the morning, we arrived in Jasic village, and the villagers warmly welcomed us. They provided us with some rooms in some private homes, and then we settled there for a while, rested, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After the FARK's arrival in Jasic, were you visited by Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not certain as to when. It was a couple of hours later of the same day. Maybe after three, four hours Mr. Haradinaj came, together with four or five other officers. He visited us, he entered inside, and he talked with our officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the other officers that Mr. Haradinaj came with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haradinaj and another officer, whose name was Maloku. I'm not sure about his pseudonym, but I had met him before in Tirana, had a coffee with him, so I knew him as Mr. Naim Maloku. Mr. Maloku is a career officer. He has graduated from the military academy, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Which military academy was that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say the "military academy," I mean the Defence Academy, as it was called then, not the police academy. At least this is how I knew its name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Defence Academy, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the former Yugoslavia. We didn't have any police academy in Kosova, so they would be either in Sarajevo or in some other cities of the former Yugoslavia; in Belgrade or in Zagreb, Ljubljana. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Were you present when Mr. Haradinaj came to Jasic that first day that the FARK arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Jasic but not in the very room where officers sat. And when he came, Mr. Haradinaj came with his officers and talked with our officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that was said in that room?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Before the witness answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Afterwards, yes, because everything that was said --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He was just about to carry on. Just so we're clear, the question, "did you hear anything that was said in the room," is ambiguous. In other words, did you hear it or did you hear later about what was said when someone told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if it's ambiguous. From the answer of the witness, at least, it appears that he clearly distinguished between hearing at the moment, but we'll ask him to answer the question. But I'm not a native speaker, Mr. Emmerson, I have to admit that. I think the witness -- could you please repeat your answer. You said: "Afterwards, yes," and then you said "because everything that was said," and then you were interrupted. Please complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answer to the question made of me, I tried to give an answer. During the time Mr. Haradinaj came there, along with his accompanying officers, he didn't come to meet the soldiers. He came to meet with the officers. The soldiers were accommodated in three private houses; whereas, the officers were in another house. Every soba room for men has an antechamber. Some people were sitting in this antechamber and some were inside. Mr. Haradinaj came to meet the officers. I could not go there and sit with them and talk. It was not my right to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you started saying something about what you heard afterwards. Do I understand your answer that you were not able to hear the conversation that took place between Mr. Haradinaj and your commanders, but that you learned about it later; if so, please tell us what you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true. That's why I said it was none of my duty to have anything to do with him. Mr. Haradinaj talked with our commanders, and then we learned of talk that had gone on among them; Mr. Haradinaj and our officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what was that talk? Please tell us what was said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to tell here what I heard because I wasn't present. Mr. Haradinaj had told our officers that, You are not welcome here. You can go back to where you came from. Kosova doesn't need you. You must go back immediately. If you don't, we will do this and that to you. It wasn't a good meeting. We expected quite another sort of meeting. And among what he told our officers was, If you don't go back to where you came from, we can fight together, but we are not going to fight the enemy. First, we are going to fight you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said the words: "If you don't -- if you don't go back immediately, we will do this and that to you." What exactly, if you know, did Mr. Haradinaj say to your leaders during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the witness can't know that. All the witness can do is relate the hearsay that was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Guy-Smith, isn't it perfectly clear that whatever the witness tells us now is hearsay. So we would not understand it any other way, in view of the earlier answers of the witness. And I think it -- this objection or this comment really does not add to the -- does not assist the Chamber in better understanding the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the Chamber's comment, but the question, as framed, certainly doesn't do it either, and it confuses the issue. And if the question is made to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not confused by the way the question was put. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, when you said earlier that Mr. Haradinaj said: "If you don't go back immediately, we will do this and that to you," can you be more specific. What do you mean by the words "this and that"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I was trying to be brief. That's why I said that. During the meeting between Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Tahir Zemaj and other officers, what was said was that, You don't need to come to Kosova. You have go back where you came from. Kosova doesn't need you. Kosova doesn't need the armed forces of the Republic of Kosovo or FARK. If you don't go back, we will fight you. We will not fight the enemy. We will leave the enemy, and we will fight you. So what I understood by that is that they would fight us; and then, if they had time, they would fight the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, in your 2002 statement to the Office of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Counsel, this is at page 5, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: -- you say that, and I'm quoting now from your statement to OTP: "Mr. Haradinaj said: 'If you don't go, we'll kill you all.'" Is that an accurate quote of your memory of what Mr. Haradinaj said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Kearney, I take it that you intended to ask the witness whether that was an accurate quote of his memory of what he was told about what Mr. Haradinaj said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: That's true and I stand corrected, and I'll rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Kearney does and leaving that issue of clarification to the side for the moment. As a general proposition, I'm not sure about the propriety of the practice of putting to a witness being called by the Prosecution passages from his statement that are not in a 92 ter form, unless we are in either a memory-refreshing situation or a hostile-witness situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a situation where this witness did make this statement now almost five years ago. It's a quote from his statement. I'm simply presenting it to him and seeing if it refreshes his memory as to what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether you have already sufficiently explored whether, without this refreshment of the memory, this evidence could be elicited is certainly subject to doubt. So therefore, would you please be cautious in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, those words that I just stated to you from your 2002 statement, do they refresh your memory as to what you were told Mr. Haradinaj said during this meeting in Jasic in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is no indication that the witness's memory needs to be refreshed. The witness has testified precisely as to what he recalls the statement; and if it is not being used for that purpose, then it is being used for purposes of impeachment, which raises the question that Mr. Emmerson raised a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can respond very briefly. We started this inquiry because the witness said "this and that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Obviously, the words "this and that" were not spoken by Mr. Haradinaj back in 1998. I'm just simply trying to specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think what the Defence emphasises is that there's no problem with further specification, but that should be done, first of all, by asking the witness -- let me just check exactly what the course of the answers were. One second, please. Yes, Mr. Kearney. You asked specification of the "this and that." The witness answered that question, but it appears that you think he could say more about it; and without first exploring whether the witness could add something to the specification he already gave, you immediately led him to his 2002 statement where at that moment perhaps the appropriate course of questioning would have been to further explore whether the witness would like to add anything to what the specification he gave, the specification being that they would fight the FARK rather than the enemy at that moment. But perhaps -- yes. Witness, when you said that the gist of the conversation was related to you as being that they, that is, Mr. Haradinaj's people, would fight you first and only then the enemy, did they in any way specify on how they would fight you? What would they do in fighting you? Was that related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us then in what terms, as you understood, this was explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, I was told that if we did not go back to Albania, Mr. Haradinaj, together with his officers and soldiers under his command, would fight us first and then the Serb forces. With this I mean they would kill us all first and then fight the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I think that this is more or less what the Defence had in mind as the proper course of further exploring the matter without already refreshing the memory of the witness. Of course, I do not know to what extent the earlier attempt to refresh the memory has influenced the answers of the witness, but this is at least perhaps the proper way of examining the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, you said that you expected a different meeting earlier between Mr. Haradinaj and your leadership. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only me, but everybody, the officers and the soldiers were looking forward to meeting the other soldiers and talking to them. It was unbelievable the way that they welcomed us. We thought that they would cooperate with us and do the same as the village of Jasic did. That was completely the opposite of what we expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: As a result of this visit by Mr. Haradinaj, did the FARK forces leave the village of Jasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FARK forces, of course, had to leave because we had come to Kosovo to do something else, not to fight with Mr. Haradinaj. That's why we tried to avoid a conflict or a bloodshed between brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, I think the army remained there for a week, maybe seven or eight days, and then we had to arrange for another place, a safer place to go. Mr. Tahir Zemaj and Commander Ceku discussed this amongst each other and decided that we had to go to another village in order to avoid conflict with Mr. Haradinaj. So myself, Mr. Ceku, and a couple of other soldiers, we went looking for a safer village - if I could call it that - in order to avoid the bloodshed with Mr. Haradinaj. And we were able to find four houses in the village of Izniq in Decani municipality. We then told Mr. Zemaj by telephone, satellite telephone, that we had found a place. We were helped immensely by the people in the Izniq village, the representatives of the village. So after we spoke with Mr. Zemaj, we -- it was decided that all the soldiers would come in the direction of Pacaj village. And myself and Sali Ceku and the two soldiers who were with us, we would wait for them Pacaj; and then together we would go to the village of Isniq. This was the movement that was expected to happen because there was no other way. We wanted to avoid the worst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can I interrupt and ask. The village of Isniq, how do you spell that village, with I-s or I-r?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It's I-s-n-i-q, where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And Your Honour makes a good point. My next question was going to be:

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Is this a different village than Irzniq?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are two different villages. There is a village called Irzniq and the other is Isniq. These are two villages in the same municipality, and I said we settled in the village of Isniq.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness also tell us where we find Pacaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Pacaj, if I understood your question correctly, this village is close to the main road Peje-Gjakove-Decane, but it is in the territory of the municipality of Gjakove. I mean the main road Decane-Gjakove divides Heric from Pacaj. That is the road I mean. But, however, this is a village in the municipality of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, after you moved to Isniq, were you at some point given an assignment involving this village you've been talking about of Pacaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, if you could repeat the question, because it's not clear to me. As I said, from Pacaj, we went to Isniq. If you mean after we went to Isniq, yes, I can give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring specifically to now the 4th of July of 1998, if that helps you. On that date, did you leave the village of Isniq and go somewhere or attempt to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the 4th of July, if I'm not mistaken, so the 4th of July, Mr. Tahir Zemaj -- I'm sorry. I think I overlooked something that I have to say. While we went to Isniq, two officers remained there, Agim Ramadani and Rrustem Berisha, with three soldiers. And during our stay in Isniq, we were in contact with Mr. Berisha and Mr. Ramadani - I mean the officers were - and we were told that some weaponry had come from Albania to Jasic. Whether it had arrived or was expected to arrived, I was not sure. So somebody had to go to Pacaj to await that consignment of weaponry. It was said that from Papaj, which is in Albania, the consignment had arrived in Jasic, but then I would await for that consignment in Pacaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there to catch up with you for a moment. You said several names. These weapons that we're talking about, they came into Kosovo from a village in Albania called Papaj, is that right, P-a-p-a-j?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Papaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And they were headed into Kosovo into the village of Pacaj, P-a-c-a-j. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, via Jasic. The village of Papaj is in Albania; from Papaj, the consignment would go to Jasic, then the people who brought the consignment had to rest for a while. From Jasic, the consignment would be transported to Pacaj, and we would await for the consignment there. It was considered that Pacaj was a safer village because there were no Serb forces in the area. However, we also wanted to avoid a conflict with KLA and Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 29, could you please slow down in your answers because the interpreters have difficulties in following your speed of speech. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney. I must admit that Pacaj, I have not found it yet on any map, although I tried hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I was just going to ask a question which may help the Trial Chambers in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: This village of Pacaj is south-west of the village of Jasic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Pacaj, if you have a map, maybe I could help you more; however, the main road Decane-Gjakove divides the village of Pacaj with the village of Heric. It goes between these villages. If you go from Decani to Gjakove, Heric is on the left side and Pacaj on the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So Witness 29, on the 4th of July, 1998, you were given the task to travel from Isniq to Papaj [sic] to pick up weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, because these names are similar to each other and may be confused, my task was to go to Pacaj and not Papaj. The same way we confused Irzniq and Isniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And I stand corrected. My apologies to both the witness and the Trial Chambers. In any event, please tell us how you made that journey and who you made it with, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of July, 1998, Commander Zemaj and Commander Ceku invited me to go to their room, where they were staying, and told me to go to the village of Pacaj to await this consignment of weapons that was coming from Albania. Mr. Ceku wanted to come with me as well, but I did not think it was appropriate for him to come because every movement of our senior officers, Mr. Zemaj, Mr. Ceku, was probably not safe for them. That's why I didn't want them to come with me. And Mr. Ceku agreed not to come and told me to choose three soldiers to go with me on this assignment. I became a kind of person responsible for that task, that assignment. I was not a commander, just the person responsible. I was given three soldiers. I decided on the soldiers myself. Can I give the name, or do you think it's not proper to give the name now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldier was called Idriz Ukehaxhaj from Carrabreg in the municipality of Decane, and he also owned a car, a small car. I don't know the make, I can't remember now, but it was his own property, his private car. I asked this Ukehaxhaj to come and speak with me. I thought that it would be easier for us to move through those villages by his car, and Ukehaxhaj agreed. I also needed two other soldiers, and I told Ukehaxhaj, "Could you go and get two other soldiers?" He went, got two soldiers. One was called Petrit Lokaj. He was from the village of Poberxhe in the Decane municipality. I think now he lives in the town of Decane. The other, Azem Gashi, is from Peje municipality. And we all agreed to travel together to go on this assignment. Towards the evening hours, Idriz went and got his car. In the meantime, one of the owners of one of the houses where we were staying said that he wanted to come with us because he wanted to visit his daughter in the village of Junik and wanted to see how she was. Of course, it was wartime and everybody wanted to see how their people were. We had room in the car so we told him that he could come. We also asked his officers whether he could and they said yes. So we started, we set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You indicated that it was not safe for Commander Ceku -- or in your opinion, it was not safe for Commander Ceku to travel. Why was that? Why was it not safe for him to travel, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the movement involved a risk from the village where we were to the other village. The situation was not stable. We wanted to avoid the conflict with Mr. Haradinaj. We thought that we would have a friendly talk with Mr. Haradinaj, and I thought that I myself could have such a friendly talk with Mr. Haradinaj, rather than the officer, because we had been friends. We had been neighbours, brothers I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: So your fear for the safety of Mr. Ceku came from Mr. Haradinaj. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I have to give briefer answers. The whole problem was we didn't want something to happen to us from Mr. Haradinaj. We didn't want to risk anybody's life from Mr. Haradinaj and the soldiers of Mr. Haradinaj. And because I thought I knew Mr. Haradinaj very well, I had met him during my visits to Kosovo, I thought I could talk with him. And I thought it would be better if I was responsible for that journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a follow-up question to what you just said. We talked at length about your ten trips into Kosovo in 1998 before the formal entry of the FARK forces. During some of those visits, did you actually meet with Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one case when I met Mr. Haradinaj. We talked with each other. It was a very friendly, brotherly conversation. We discussed several things about the situation. He told me, Things are going like this. Maybe in the future we will be even better prepared. It was a very good meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you know what date that meeting was? What time it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very sure. That's why I don't want to give you dates, accurate dates. Although, I can't remember it. Maybe Mr. Haradinaj can help us with that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us if it was before March 24th or after March 24th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the 24th of March, but I can't give you an exact date. I don't want to give you a date and then find out that it wasn't the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Do you remember where the meeting itself was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we met in the birthplace of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where that is, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His native village is Gllogjan village in the municipality of Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And you said you discussed things during this meeting with Mr. Haradinaj. Do you remember what specifically it was that you discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but we discussed about the things that we were preparing over there, that things were going well. We were waiting for the moment when we would enter Kosova, and Mr. Haradinaj agreed. And when we parted with each other, we were two people who were very close to each other parting with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you said you were -- you discussed the moment when you were waiting to enter Kosova, are you referring to when the FARK forces would enter Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I told him that preparations are underway and that soon we would -- that the armed forces of the Republic of Kosova, albeit FARK, would enter Kosova. We will join our forces. We will fight the enemy together, and he welcomed these conversations, seemed to be very content with it, at least that's my impression of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: During this conversation you had with him, did he state what his rank was? What his position was at that time? Did you know what it was? Can you tell us anything about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This -- another time there were no ranks but he was a commander because with us in Kosova -- to us, ranks are the ranks given to you when you are a professional officer, when you are in an academy, or so. Maybe he has. I apologise to him if he has, but to me he was a commander. But I don't know if he had ranks; of this, I'm not certain. However, I knew him as a co-villager and as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I want to move back now, if we may, to the 4th of July of 1998, and I want to ask you what time of day was it that you set out with these other three FARK soldiers you described and the civilian in Mr. Ukehaxhaj's car?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kearney, I see that we're now moving back to the 4th of July. I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps that might be a moment for a break, and then after the break we could continue with the 4th of July. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, you may proceed. The Chamber would like to give as a guidance to the parties, that, of course, it's highly appreciated if the parties draw the attention to the Chamber of risks of confusion; at the same time, sometimes if there is a small risk of confusion, first of all, it does not always materialise. Second, if there's confusion, of course, the Chamber, unlike a member of a jury, could easily try to clarify what might confuse them. So, therefore, this is not to tell the parties, Don't draw our attention to confusion, but don't do it too quickly, and perhaps now and then rely on the abilities of this Chamber to have confusion moved aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have -- I certainly have not been moving quickly and the confusion, less of a concern is the confusion of the Chamber and more is the concern of the confusion of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The record always reflects what is said, so there could be no confusion. But this is just that I hope the parties got the message. Please proceed, Mr. Kearney.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Witness 29, when we left off you, were just leaving on your -- from Isniq on your trip to Pacaj to get the weapons. I want to ask you: During that journey after you left Isniq, did you come to a stop in any village along your way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After we left Isniq village, we passed through several villages and stopped at the village. I can tell you the name of the village, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped at Irzniq village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Why did you stop there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped there for two reasons: One was that I had to get a military uniform, and the other was that the person who was with us, not the soldier, wanted to buy something for his grandson whom he wanted to visit at his daughter's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Irzniq, was there a KLA presence in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But even along the way, we saw members of the KLA. But also in Irzniq village when we stopped the car, I left in the direction of the place where I was supposed to get the uniform; whereas, that person with the three soldiers remained in the store to have something to drink and to buy what he wanted to buy. I went to the village command in the meantime, and the commander -- there was a commander of the village, whose name was Maxhun Cekaj. He was responsible for the village. He was also a reserve major in the Yugoslav Army. I got a paper, a piece of paper, from him to make things easier for me on the way, and then I left to get the uniform. In the meantime, we met Mr. Haradinaj in the centre of Irzniq village. Mr. Haradinaj just arrived in a four-wheel-drive, a big car. He was accompanied by Togeri, who was most known at that time, and he stopped the car nearby our car. He stopped. It was quite normal act. He lowered his window. I did the same. We talked. I can't relate here exactly what we said verbatim, but the most important thing was that he said, "It's good to see you. When you are in Kosova, we will see each other. We will talk." That's it. To me, I took it as a normal occurrence, as in fact I expected him to behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there for a moment, please. You said the village commander was a gentleman you knew to be a reserve major in the Yugoslav Army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did he have any, to your knowledge, professional background or training in the military or in defence studies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't be precise, 100 per cent precise, but I know he was a major, not an active officer in the Yugoslav Army. There was a part of the Yugoslav Army described as reservists or territorial defence forces, which were organised on the level of municipality in Kosova but I think also in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And yet on this day, the 4th of July, 1998, he was a village commander for the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about Maxhun Cekaj, the commander of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said you received from him some kind of document. Is that correct? Can you please tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we described it as a document, but in fact it was a piece of paper, handwritten. It didn't have any kind of letterhead or something like this. It was a piece of paper; whereby, I was, in this case, authorised, name and last name given, to travel from Irzniq village to Pacaj village to get a shipment of arms. And along with him there are also three other soldiers, things like this. It was a paper that I might show in places where we deemed it appropriate to make our passage easier by means of such a document. It was not an order, per se, but it was a handwritten paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Now, you said sometime after that Mr. Haradinaj and a gentleman named Togeri arrived in a vehicle. This person that you called Togeri, do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't come to our car; but when I was going to the place to get the uniform, Mr. Haradinaj and Togeri stopped their car - so maybe this is the right description - then Mr. Haradinaj stopped the car, lowered the window. He was driving the car, and he was accompanied by Togeri, who was the person we knew most. Idriz Balaj is his name. I don't know where he came from, but not from Decane municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question put to you was simply whether you would know the real name of the person you called Togeri. Could you please focus your answers exactly on the question. If Mr. Kearney would like to know more, he'll certainly ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Had you seen this person, Togeri, or Idriz Balaj, before this date, on July 4th of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen him two or three times, but he was known all over by the name of Togeri, by the pseudonym. I had met him, yes, two or three times before. I had not talked with him. I just had seen him in the street moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And when you say that in the vehicle with him was Mr. Haradinaj, you're talking about Ramush Haradinaj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, yes. He was on the driver's seat. He was driving, but he was accompanied by Togeri. At the moment that he spoke -- that he stopped the car - if I can go on - he didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please go on. Do you want to finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can, yes. Then I greeted him, he greeted me. He said, It's good that you are here. And he said what I mentioned earlier. We parted our ways. He went his way. I went to the place I was supposed to gather the uniform; then after a couple of minutes - I can't be precise - I got the information that at the place where I had left the soldiers, Mr. Haradinaj had gone there, not Ramush Haradinaj, but Daut Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hate to interject, but really, at this point, there's no question pending. The witness has moved on to a narrative answer with regard to what he was doing that way. If that's a way the Chamber chooses to proceed, so be it; but I think it causes a series of difficulties in terms of knowing what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kearney, I already earlier tried to -- I tried to keep the witness closer to the question. So, Witness, would you please always carefully listen to the question. It's not -- it might be important what you say, but it might not be exactly what Mr. Kearney would like to hear from you as further detail. So please focus on the question and then, Mr. Kearney, you know how to deal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I'm just mindful of the time-limit, and that's why I was allowing the witness to proceed. But I'll be mindful of the Trial Chamber's directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we do not know exactly what your next questions are. So you are the one to be best able to see if the witness gives further details, if he goes in the direction you would go anyhow or whether it's something different. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You indicated at some point after you went to get your uniform, you received some information that there was some trouble involving Daut Haradinaj, is that correct; and if that's true, please tell us what that trouble was, what you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And what was it that you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time, I was getting the uniform, one of the brothers came and told me that two persons have come to that store. One is called Daut Haradinaj, the other Togeri, Idriz Balaj, and they were trying to get those persons I left at the store with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: The FARK soldiers, are those the persons you left at the store you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely those; the three soldiers, and the fourth person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: After you received this information, did you go back to the store yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went immediately without losing any time. After two, three minutes, four minutes, as fast as I could, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Please tell us what happened when you got back to the store.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I arrived at the store, I saw Daut Haradinaj with Togeri, Idriz Balaj, in two cars. Both were large vehicles, 4-by-4 as we called them then, and they were threatening the soldiers to get them with them in their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: When you say "to get them with them," what do you mean? What were they -- what was Mr. Balaj or Mr. Haradinaj saying to them that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, both were in uniform; Mr. Haradinaj - I mean Daut Haradinaj - and Balaj, Togeri. They were talking with the soldiers and threatening them to get them into their car. I mean they wanted them to -- to get into the car and to drive them to the place they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: And did they say where it was they wanted to drive the FARK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there and Daut saw me, he said, "You and them, both, and all of them are going to come with us in our car, and we will take you to the staff in Gllogjan village, to Ramush Haradinaj."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: What tone was this said in? Was this said in a friendly tone, a hostile tone? Describe that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, with the exception of the tone used by Mr. Ramush Haradinaj, which was a very friendly tone; in this case, their tone was threatening, very harsh tone. It was a very bad moment I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: You said that Daut Haradinaj and Idriz Balaj were uniformed. Did they have weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had gotten out of their cars and had a pistol on their belt and a knife on their chest, hanging on their chests. I don't know how exactly that was placed in a belt, or I don't know what, holster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
utterances.text: Did either one of them use their weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/29 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one moment, because they kept insisting for us to come along with them into their cars and to take us to Gllogjan village, to Ramush Haradinaj. And I refused with -- I didn't want to go with them because I had already seen Mr. Haradinaj. I said, "Okay. I will come and meet Mr. Haradinaj, but I will come with my own car." Mr. Haradinaj took out his pistol and shot in the air, and it was a threatening gesture, as if to force us to go into their cars, but I did -- I refused. I said, "Okay, I'll come, but with my own car."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEARNEY
